1:
Whose idea the spies were is the first question, since Deuteronomy says the people asked and this chapter says God commanded. Henry gives the sharpest account of it. The motion came from the people and was the fruit of their unbelief: they would not take God's word that the land was good, and had a better opinion of their own politics than of God's wisdom. It was absurd to spy out a land God had already spied out for them, and to enquire the way when he had undertaken to show it. Moses, perhaps not seeing the unbelief at the bottom of it, consulted God, who bade him gratify them and let them walk in their own counsels. Gill says the scheme was of their own devising and that God rather permitted than approved it, giving Jarchi's paraphrase of the answer: send men according to thy mind; I do not command thee, but if thou pleasest send. Wesley traces the request to diffidence of the promise. Ellicott denies there is any inconsistency between the two accounts, since it would be wholly unlike Moses to act in a matter of this weight without seeking direction; and he warns that the command no more proves the errand was God's own than the later command to Balaam proved that God approved his journey.

Keil and Delitzsch set the errand out plainly: from Kadesh in the desert of Paran, by God's command and at the people's wish, men went to explore the way in and the nature of the land, its cities and its population. The choice of them is where Calvin finds the care of the arrangement. Had they all been drawn from one tribe their fidelity might have been suspected by the rest, so God would have every tribe assured by its own witness, lest a tribe passed over should object that the messengers were chosen in contempt of it. They were to be men of personal dignity besides, since obscure men are easily discredited. Both precautions failed, and Calvin draws the lesson from the failure: there is no counsel so wise and salutary that the wickedness of men cannot pervert it, and the providence that took such care left the people the more inexcusable. Clarke and Ellicott both note that these twelve were not the tribal princes of the census, the names being different; Ellicott adds that Levi is absent, having no inheritance to come, the number being made up by dividing Joseph into Ephraim and Manasseh. Henry sees the honour turn against them, the quality of the men making the evil report the more believed.

Calvin reads the roll that follows as a monument rather than a record. The names are enumerated in perpetual remembrance of their ignominy, two excepted, because it was just that their crime be handed down to every age and the infamy of their perfidiousness never blotted out, since they endeavoured as far as in them lay to bring to nothing the promise and the grace of God. He adds a second lesson from the same failure: however men who seemed to be pillars may totter or fall outright, our own minds must still be supported by faith. On the one name in the list that was changed he and Henry agree. Calvin holds that Moses named the son of Nun in the spirit of prophecy, not by blindness of affection but with his tongue directed by God, to commend beforehand the man who was to be the minister of their preservation; ambition is so rash that men who invent titles of honour for themselves are commonly disappointed of them. Henry sets the two names against each other, Oshea being a prayer for salvation, Save thou, and Joshua a promise of it, He will save — so near, he says, is the relation between prayers and promises, for prayers prevail for promises and promises encourage prayers.
4:
The roll of the twelve is mostly bare names, and the commentators stop only where a name raises a question. Ellicott halts at Caleb, who is called the Kenizzite in three later places. Since the Kenizzites appear among the Canaanite tribes and Kenaz is an Edomite name, it has been conjectured from this that Caleb was of foreign origin and had been incorporated into the tribe of Judah; but Ellicott thinks the conjecture rests on insufficient grounds. At Ephraim he suspects a displacement of the text, since Zebulun would naturally have followed Issachar and Ephraim been joined to Manasseh, as they stand in the census, and the appearance of the name of Joseph on either side of the gap supports him. Wesley notices what that name is doing there. Joseph elsewhere stands for Ephraim and here for Manasseh, and he wonders whether it is set down to aggravate the sin of a ruler who so basely degenerated from his noble ancestor. Clarke pauses at Sethur only to dismiss what has been built on it. The name comes from a verb meaning to hide, so that it signifies hidden or mysterious, and its letters add up to six hundred and sixty-six; it would have been strange, he says, had the many searches after that number found nothing to their purpose here. Then he asks what use such expositions can be to any subject of history or theology. Gill observes that the list is summed up again at the close so that the names may be marked, standing as they do to the disgrace of the greater number and to the honour of two.

The one alteration Moses made is to the name of his own minister. Clarke gives the sense of both forms, Hoshea meaning saved, or a saviour, and Jehoshua he shall save, a letter of the incommunicable name having been added to the old word; and he reports the opinion of some that the change followed the victory over Amalek. Ellicott will not have it fixed here at all. The text does not distinctly say the change was made on this occasion, and it may have happened earlier and been only confirmed now, as with the renaming of Israel and of Bethel; or else the new name was used proleptically in the passages of Exodus and Numbers where it appears already. Wesley keeps to the meaning rather than the date, taking Oshea for a desire of salvation and Joshua for a promise of it, and reading the change as a prophecy both of his succession to Moses in the government and of the success of his arms. He ends where the name leads, since Joshua is the same name as Jesus, and the man who saved God's people from the powers of Canaan was a type of the one who saves them from the powers of hell.
17:
The route is laid out in two stages. Ellicott renders the first not southward but by the Negeb, the south country, which formed the transition from the desert to cultivated land and was fitter for grazing than for tillage. Wesley explains why they began there: it was the nearest part and the worst, dry and desert, and so the part they could enter and pass through with least notice taken of them. The mountain is the hill country held by the Hittites, Jebusites and Amorites, which Deuteronomy calls the mount of the Amorites because that tribe was the strongest, though Ellicott allows that the word here may point to the particular mountain nearest the camp. Wesley has them go up into the high country and down again into the valleys, so taking a survey of the whole. Keil and Delitzsch report how far they actually went, from the desert of Zin, which was the northern edge of the great desert of Paran, to Rehob near Hamath — the land in its whole extent from south to north.

Calvin explains why the questions Moses asked hang together. A barren country cannot support a large population, and the healthfulness of a place may be inferred from the vigour of the people living in it, so the enquiries about the men and about the soil answer each other. He thinks Moses insisted chiefly on the goodness of the land and its abundance of fruit, and that the main point was to let its pleasantness allure them to go up and take it; though he allows that God may also have meant them forewarned that they would have strong enemies to deal with, lest the sudden sight of such men should dismay them. Ellicott notes that the word rendered see is better inspect, the very word used of the priest inspecting a leper. Clarke divides the charge into its parts, what sort of country it is and how situated, and whether the people are healthy and hardy men or little and weak. Gill adds the questions of air and climate and water, which he says stood first in the intention though they come second in the text. On the cities Ellicott prefers camps to tents, meaning open villages set against fortified places, and Wesley says such unwalled villages lie exposed to an enemy as tents do. The last question is of the soil, which Clarke says would be known by the timber and by the fruit; and Ellicott observes that the season was right for the test, since the first grapes ripen in Palestine as early as July or August, long before the vintage.
21:
They went the whole length of the land, and Henry supposes they went it carefully. Probably they did not travel as one body, lest they be suspected and taken up, but divided into several companies and passed as wayfaring men. Clarke and Wesley distinguish this desert of Zin from the Sin of the earlier march, which lay near Egypt, while this bordered on the promised land. Clarke traces the circuit: from Kadesh-barnea they went up nearly along the Jordan to Rehob at the northern extremity, and returned through the middle of the country by the borders of the Sidonians and Philistines, coming at last by Hebron to the valley of Eshcol. Ellicott identifies Rehob with the Beth-rehob of Judges, near Dan, and notes that the entrance of Hamath was afterwards fixed as Israel's northern boundary. Calvin thinks their industry deserves its credit, since in so short a time they examined the whole country, and did it in the hottest part of the year; thus far, he says, they faithfully executed what was entrusted to them.

At Hebron the account turns singular, and the commentators notice it. Ellicott points out that the Hebrew has he came, not they came, and allows that the twelve may not have kept together, one only going up to Hebron. Wesley names him from Joshua: it was Caleb, the spies having divided the work and gone severally or in pairs. Gill explains the word ascended, which is used because on the return they came up again into the hill country, Hebron and the cluster belonging to the homeward journey. Henry finds the place chosen for a reason, since near it lay the field of Machpelah where the patriarchs were buried, whose bodies kept possession of the land for their posterity; and there, where they looked for their greatest encouragement, they met their greatest discouragement, for where the dead fathers held the ground for them the giants held it against them. Whether Ahiman and Sheshai and Talmai were men or clans is disputed. Ellicott reports that some take them for tribes, but observes that the same men may well have been living fifty years later, when Caleb drove these three out. Calvin knows the opinion that Anak is no proper name but a word for giants, and answers it from the close of the chapter, where Anak plainly is a man whose sons were of excessive height. Wesley makes their presence an argument for the land: the giants had chosen it to live in. Keil and Delitzsch confirm what the men would report of the country's fruit, since bunches of eight, ten and twelve pounds are still met with in Palestine, and the vineyards north of Hebron carry the finest in the land. Henry, looking ahead to what they gathered there, takes it for earnest and specimen at once, as the comforts believers have in communion with God are foretastes of the fulness of joy, by which we may see what heaven is.

The note about Zoan is read as a stroke against Egypt. Clarke identifies Zoan with Tanis, the capital of Lower Egypt, and reports the opinion that the remark was put in to humble a people who boasted the highest antiquity of any; some have thought it a marginal note which crept into the text, but every version and every manuscript yet collated has it. Wesley says the same more briefly. Ellicott places Tanis on the eastern arm of the Nile and takes it for the residence of Pharaoh in the days of Moses. Calvin draws a different inference from the same comparison. Since the Egyptians gloried in their antiquity above all nations, the verse proves that Canaan was well peopled immediately after the flood; and that in turn argues its fertility, for men free to settle where they chose would not have preferred it had the neighbouring countries been richer.
23:
The one thing they carried home was the cluster, and the commentators set about sizing it. Clarke gathers travellers' reports from several countries: Pliny speaks of African bunches larger than an infant, one traveller saw bunches three quarters of an ell long at Rhodes with grapes as large as plums, and another weighed bunches at Damascus at above five and forty pounds. Then he adds the point that gives the story its force. The Egyptian grape is small, and it was the only grape the Israelites knew, so the fruit of Hebron would have struck them as more extraordinary than it strikes us. Ellicott is the more restrained, putting the largest clusters ordinarily grown in Palestine at ten or twelve pounds, though he cites a Syrian bunch of nineteen pounds raised in England which four labourers carried more than twenty miles, two at a time, slung upon a staff. Both he and Clarke conclude that the staff here was used less for the weight than to bring the fruit home unbruised, so that the people might have a fair specimen; Wesley allows either reason, the length of the way or the keeping of it whole. Gill notes that the valley cannot have borne the name at the time, since it was called Eshcol afterwards in memory of what was done there, and Ellicott adds that the verse explains why Israel so called it without settling whether it had carried the name already, from Eshcol the brother of Mamre.

The return closes the errand. Keil and Delitzsch give the shape of what was said: the men came back to Kadesh in forty days and reported the great fertility of the land, pointing to the fruit they carried, and then turned on a single word — only that the people are strong, the cities fortified and very great, and we saw the children of Anak there. Calvin fastens on that word. Everything the ten said was true and had been ascertained by them, and at first sight their report contains nothing to blame; yet they spoke of the difficulties in terms designed to turn the people back, and so produced the very effect Moses had hoped to prevent. They had not openly lied, but they were wanting in sincerity, laying a foundation of good faith in order to be the better able to deceive; and Calvin draws the warning that crafty men gain nothing with God by covering deceit with tortuous prevarications, so that a man who would have his speech approved must lay aside such evasions and speak simply and from the heart. He notices too that they thundered out the names of several nations to increase the alarm. Wesley wonders at the forty days from the other side, that the people had patience to wait so long when they were ready to enter and had every assurance the divine power could give; they distrusted God and chose to be held in suspense by their own counsels rather than rest on his promise. Ellicott says only that the time allowed a full and careful exploration.
26:
Where they came back to is disputed on the map. Ellicott sets out the two identifications of Kadesh, Robinson's with a spring in the Arabah north of Mount Hor, and a rival one some sixty miles west of it. Wesley is concerned with a different confusion, warning that this Kadesh is not the one in the wilderness of Zin which Israel reached only in the fortieth year, since they stood here in the second, before the sentence of the forty years was passed. Gill notes that the men went straight to Moses and Aaron before their own tents. Henry marks where the account divides, for the messengers return but do not agree, and he thinks the majority report a judgment as much as a failure: it is a righteous thing with God to give men up to strong delusions who will not receive his truth in the love of it, and Israel had trusted the judgment of men above the word they had. Yet the report opens with a concession. The spies could not deny the land was fruitful, the cluster being an ocular demonstration of it; Ellicott observes that they took up the very words of the promise at the bush. Henry makes the concession serve: thus even out of the mouth of adversaries will God be glorified, and the truth of his promise attested.

Everything turns on the word that follows. Gill puts the objection as the spies meant it: however desirable the country, the strength of its inhabitants lay against all hope of possessing it, men of large and some of prodigious stature. Ellicott notes that the discouragement was worked by two things, the fortified cities and the gigantic inhabitants. Henry says nothing in their report served their ill purpose so well as the giants, on whom they laid great stress, speaking as though they were ready to tremble at the mention of them. Clarke finds the performance strange in men who had just done what they did. It is astonishing that men so dastardly should have had courage to risk their persons in searching the land; probably, though destitute of valour, they had a sufficiency of cunning, and that carried them through. Alone in the company, he says, the conduct of Joshua and Caleb was magnanimous and worthy of the cause they were embarked in. Keil and Delitzsch note that tidings of this character were bound to excite the people.

The list of nations that closes the report is read two ways. Wesley takes it as a catalogue of obstacles arranged by compass point. The Amalekites hold the south, where Israel must enter, and having once come out into the wilderness to fight will the more certainly oppose them now; the hill country to the south-east cannot be entered without great difficulty, both from the valour of the people and from the advantage the mountains give them; and the sea meant is not the midland sea but the salt sea, so that these guard the eastern approach as the others guard the southern. Gill agrees that the Amalekites were named though they were no Canaanites, being neighbours to them, enemies to Israel since Rephidim, and lying nearest the camp. Henry reads the same geography the other way about. It is true the Canaanites were strong, but they were dispersed: some in the south and some in the mountains, so that by reason of their distance they could not soon get together, and by reason of their divided interests could not long keep together. He will not excuse the spies of cowardice even on human probabilities, since six hundred thousand effective men made as formidable an army as was ever brought into the field, and a plentiful country would subsist it. As for the giants, he says, their overgrown stature would only make them the better mark, and the bulkiest men have not always the best mettle.
30:
Caleb has to quiet the people before he can answer the spies, and the commentators reconstruct the scene from that. Gill takes the murmuring to have begun already, the people speaking against Moses for bringing them out of Egypt and feeding them with hopes of a country they were never likely to enjoy; in their wrath, he thinks, they may have been making up to him with threats, and Caleb restrained them by signifying that he had something to say — a man they would hear, being himself one of the spies and of the leading tribe. Calvin reasons the same way from the word: there would have been no need to restrain violence unless the contention had waxed warm, so much must have been said on both sides that is passed over in silence. Ellicott observes how much the narrative leaves out, since Joshua concurred with Caleb, as the next chapter shows, and Moses himself remonstrated earnestly, as Deuteronomy shows, and neither appears here. Wesley and Calvin both account for the silence about Joshua. Wesley thinks Caleb spoke first and most, and could do it with more weight, being presumed the more impartial of the two, since Joshua as Moses' minister might be thought to say only what his master would like. Calvin holds that Caleb spoke for both and that Joshua was prudently silent lest a tumultuous altercation arise; and he sees the honesty of Moses in it, who by preferring Caleb diminishes the praise due to his own servant.

What Caleb actually says is weighed word by word. Wesley notices that he does not say, let us go up and conquer it, but let us go up and possess it, looking on the conquest as good as done and leaving nothing to do but enter and take what their great Lord was ready to give; thus, he says, the difficulties that lie in the way of salvation vanish before a lively faith. Calvin grounds the confidence where Caleb grounded it, on the promise: relying on it he believed they would succeed and boldly foretold it, while the others never took into account that a people with the banner of the Lord before them would come into the inheritance. The answer of the ten is the flat contrary. Keil and Delitzsch state it plainly, that his companions were of the opposite opinion and declared the going up impossible because the people there were stronger than Israel. Gill notes that all of them said it but Joshua. Wesley sees what the words amount to: in denying the strength they question the power and the truth and the goodness of God, of all which they had such ample testimonies.
32:
The ten now say something they had not said before, and it is the one clause in the chapter the commentators cannot agree on. Gill marks the change as evidence against them: they had given a good report of the land itself, and now change their language, which shows their want of integrity and how far an opposition will carry men, to say things contrary to their own sentiments and to what they had said themselves. Calvin describes the same movement as a progress in boldness. At the outset the authors of the rebellion were ambiguous and contented themselves with obscure insinuations; now they throw aside all shame and openly oppose Caleb, which was nothing less than discrediting God's word and setting his power at naught, until in their falsehood they contradict themselves, having confessed the land rich and now declaring that it devours those who live in it. Calvin takes the phrase to mean that its cultivation was difficult and full of inconvenience. Keil and Delitzsch reject that reading by name, denying that the spies meant the inhabitants worn out with labour or the climate unwholesome, and hold instead that the land was an apple of discord, wasting its people because the surrounding nations strove for so fruitful and well-placed a country. Ellicott lays out three possibilities, a land of scarcity, an unhealthy land, or a land consumed by the strife of those contending for it, and inclines to the last. Wesley takes the second, guessing with some Hebrew writers that the spies had seen many funerals on their travels; and he adds that if they did, the cause was the singular providence of God, thinning the Canaanites before Israel by a plague or by the hornet, so that the very thing they used to discourage the people was a mercy prepared for them.

The giants are handled with more agreement and more caution. Clarke does not doubt they saw a robust and warlike race of great stature, since neither Joshua nor Caleb denies it, but he will not have a nation twelve or fourteen feet high; Goliath at about nine feet was extraordinary, and Clarke reports from his own neighbourhood two brothers above seven feet and a third of eight feet six, well proportioned men. He suggests besides that the comparison was unfair on Israel's side, the growth of the people having probably been cramped by their long and severe servitude in Egypt, which may partly account for the alarm. Ellicott notes that the word is the nephilim of Genesis, allows that such men certainly existed in Canaan, and denies there is any evidence that the inhabitants generally were of extraordinary size. Gill presses the same point harder: the spies say we saw the giants as though the land were full of them, when they had seen them at Hebron only, and there were three. On the last clause he thinks they overreached themselves, since a man may know he felt like a grasshopper but cannot know how he looked to another, and they could only guess it from being treated with contempt. Calvin would mend the sentence by inverting it, so that the sense runs: as grasshoppers are despised in our eyes, so we were looked down upon by these giants for our lowness of stature. Clarke ends by turning the whole report into a warning for preachers, who allow that the land is good and even show some of its fruit, and then discourage the people by pronouncing the enemy unconquerable; against whom, here and there, a Joshua and a Caleb stand forth.
